reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: Results from compression of the left renal vein, most often between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery (anterior nutcracker), causing venous hypertension in the left kidney
Typical features include haematuria (which may be gross), left flank or loin pain, and, in the posterior variant, retroaortic vein compression
Because the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, the raised pressure can cause pelvic congestion in women and a left varicocele in men
It should be distinguished from the anatomical 'nutcracker phenomenon' seen on imaging without symptoms, which does not by itself warrant intervention
The syndrome is more common in thin individuals with little retroperitoneal fat and can present in adolescents and young adults
Orthostatic proteinuria may accompany the haematuria in younger patients
Diagnosis combines symptoms with imaging (Doppler ultrasound, CT or MR venography) and sometimes measurement of the renocaval pressure gradient
Management ranges from conservative observation, especially in younger patients who may improve with growth and weight gain, to endovascular or surgical treatment in severe or persistent cases
reference.pathophysiology: Nutcracker syndrome arises from mechanical entrapment of the left renal vein, classically where it passes through the acute angle between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta, or, in the posterior variant, behind the aorta. Compression raises pressure within the left renal vein, producing venous congestion of the kidney. Thin-walled veins in the collecting system may rupture into the urinary space, causing haematuria, while elevated pressure transmitted to the left gonadal vein leads to pelvic congestion or varicocele. Reduced retroperitoneal and mesenteric fat, as in slim individuals, narrows the aortomesenteric angle and predisposes to the condition.
additionalDifferentials: Glomerular causes of haematuria (e.g. IgA nephropathy, thin basement membrane nephropathy)
Pelvic congestion syndrome from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Doppler ultrasound of the left renal vein to assess flow and velocity
CT or MR venography to demonstrate compression and collaterals
Cystoscopy to confirm a left-sided source of haematuria when needed
Measurement of the renocaval pressure gradient in selected cases
Urinalysis to exclude a glomerular source and assess proteinuria
redFlags: Severe or recurrent gross haematuria with anaemia
Signs of renal impairment or venous thrombosis
Symptoms that fail to improve with conservative measures over time
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally favourable; many younger patients improve spontaneously with growth or weight gain, and those needing intervention usually do well, although symptoms can be persistent and troublesome in some.
pitfalls: Treating an incidental imaging 'nutcracker phenomenon' that is not causing symptoms
Overlooking a glomerular cause of haematuria before attributing it to venous compression
Rushing to invasive treatment, particularly in adolescents who may resolve spontaneously
Failing to recognise associated pelvic congestion or varicocele as part of the syndrome
